data.content_ref: inline:The target identifies sky view factor as the single mechanism that explains both the existence of nocturnal UHI and its cross-city variation, explicitly asserting this occurs 'independently of thermal mass or anthropogenic heat.' This causal claim is empirically false. While reduced sky view factor slows radiative cooling, urban surfaces must have heat to radiate. Thermal mass determines how much daytime heat is stored and released at night; without it, surfaces would equilibrate quickly and the radiative trapping advantage would be negligible. The target's own countercondition acknowledges this ("If urban materials have very low thermal mass...there is little stored heat to trap and the geometric effect alone may be insufficient"), directly contradicting the claim that sky view factor operates independently of thermal mass. Similarly, anthropogenic heat emissions are well-documented contributors to nocturnal UHI that vary significantly across cities. By asserting sky view factor alone explains cross-city variation and explicitly excluding other factors, the target fails to answer the problem's request for what mechanism 'best explains why that night-time gap is larger in some cities than in others' — the answer requires acknowledging multiple interacting mechanisms, not a single geometric one.
